extracted.intended_audience: general readers and retail cryptocurrency investors
extracted.subtask_description: A news explainer summarizing what happened in the FTX bankruptcy and why it matters, focusing on causes (tokens, related-party risk, liquidity, governance) and consequences for customers and investors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audited financials and reliable reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Businesses should produce balance sheets several times a year that provide reliable information on assets and liabilities; FTX/related firms' balance sheets were never audited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that the balance sheets of Bankman-Fried’s firms "were never audited," meaning there is no reliable account or paper trail of what money the company had and where it went. Lack of audited financials is presented as a major red flag and contributor to the inability to ascertain funds or responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation between exchange and affiliated trading firms (no commingling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear corporate separation and no improper transfer of customer/exchange funds to related trading entities (e.g., FTX vs. Alameda Research).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece discusses reports that Alameda had used FTX funds for trading and that funds moved between FTX and Alameda; Bankman-Fried called some transfers 'internal mislabeling.' Examples include blockchain analysts tracking $400 million of assets moving out of FTX accounts. Evaluators should look for evidence of related-party transactions and clear accounting for intercompany flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Token concentration and native-token liquidity risk (FTT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on a native token (FTT) held in large amounts by affiliated entities creates concentration and liquidity risk if the token's price falls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CoinDesk-published Alameda balance sheet showed a large holding of FTT. Because FTT was minted by FTX and trading was relatively limited, a price drop (triggered by e.g., Binance selling FTT) could (and did) endanger Alameda’s solvency. Criterion: check how much an entity’s assets depend on its own token and how liquid that token is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Token issuance transparency and token supply traceability
rubrics_metrics.description: How transparent is the token's issuance and supply (can one track how many tokens exist and who holds them)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article points out FTT was "less transparent than other tokens, making it hard to track just how many tokens had been created." Lack of traceability increases counterparty and valuation risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liquidity management and withdrawal capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability of an exchange to meet customer withdrawal requests and manage sudden runs on deposits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the FTT price drop and loss of confidence, many customers rushed to withdraw assets—"billions of dollars poured out"—and FTX stopped allowing withdrawals. A good evaluator should assess liquidity buffers, withdrawal-processing robustness, and contingency plans for rapid outflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate controls, governance, and managerial competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence of effective corporate controls, trustworthy financial information, and competent management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: John Ray (who helped navigate Enron's bankruptcy) described FTX’s situation as a "complete failure of corporate controls and such a complete absence of trustworthy financial information." The article frames weak internal controls and managerial failures as central causes of the collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercompany opacity and adherence to standard financial procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether companies follow standard reporting and accounting procedures and maintain a clear paper trail for assets and transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that FTX and sister companies allegedly didn’t follow standard financial reporting procedures, making it difficult to determine how funds were handled. Criterion: presence of routine audits, reconciliations, and documented accounting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market and counterparty signals (large-holder actions and due diligence findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions by major market participants or counterparties (e.g., large sell-offs, refusal to finalize deals after due diligence) as indicators of underlying problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binance's announcement it would sell all its FTT and its later decision to back out of purchasing FTX after due diligence are presented as catalytic signals. Evaluators should monitor behavior of prominent industry actors and outcomes of third-party due diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotional claims, celebrity endorsements, and product-market fit vs. fundamentals
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which marketing, celebrity endorsements, or promises of high yields substitute for sound financial/operational fundamentals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FTX grew rapidly via high-profile marketing and celebrity endorsements, attracting customers beyond technologists. The article suggests such PR can mask operational or financial weaknesses; caution is warranted when hype outpaces transparency and controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solvency metrics and capital adequacy (funding gaps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the firm has sufficient capital/liquidity to cover obligations; existence of any reported funding shortfalls (e.g., claims FTX needed $8 billion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media reports (cited in the article) said FTX needed about $8 billion to cover the gap between what it owed and what it could pay out. The article notes the company and its founder discussed raising large sums to 'make things right.' Check for clear statements about capital shortfalls and realistic plans to cover them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and legal compliance risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure to regulatory investigations or enforcement (e.g., SEC, DOJ), which can indicate legal noncompliance or add risk post-failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports that The Wall Street Journal and the Associated Press cited sources saying FTX faced SEC and DOJ investigations. Regulatory scrutiny is both a symptom and a further risk; presence of investigations should be factored into assessments.
